utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOKO
utterances.text: May the Registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-11-T, the Prosecutor versus Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yesterday we had a few outstanding issues to be dealt with today. Maybe we should start with them before we go into the opening statements. The first issue that was outstanding was the question of discussing the guidelines and the standards governing the admission of evidence. Are there any comments from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We are agreeable to the proposed guidelines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we first came across this particular instruction yesterday. We have studied it, and we shall comply with the deadline and file a written motion on all these issues, with your permission, of course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. The next issue was relative to the length of the Prosecutor's case and the number of witnesses. The determination has to be made in terms of section -- with Rule 73 bis(C) and we really never did make that determination yesterday. Mr. Whiting, we would like to hear from you first of all on the number of witnesses that you are -- the Prosecution intends calling relating to the 92 bis issues and the 94 bis issues and see whether there isn't anything further than that that can be added to that list. Let me say that I think the Chamber is aware that the Prosecution is filing 20 92 bis statements. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have the number on the -- on my fingertips but that sounds correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That sounds correct, okay. The Chamber is concerned to make sure that the time available is used as efficiently as possible and to that end, we would like to ask you a few questions about some of the witnesses that are not necessarily on the 92 bis list, to find out if the time allocated to them cannot be further curtailed. The first one is your MM-1, your very first witness. Given the statement of agreed facts that was filed from the bar yesterday, the Chamber wanted to find out from the Prosecution whether the Prosecution is not in a position to reduce those hours for that particular witness. It seems as if the major issues that that witness is likely to testify on are already covered in the agreed facts. Is that correct or not correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's certainly true that some of the issues that the witness might touch on are covered by the agreed facts. However, I think that the number of hours that we have estimated is still nonetheless appropriate because this witness was the most important political figure in the region where the crimes occurred during 1991. He has an enormous amount of information and an enormous number of documents and evidence pertaining to -- not just to the background that is covered by the agreed facts but by -- but about the charges themselves, and in particular, the relationships among various entities, the joint criminal enterprise among very important figures within the joint criminal enterprise, which is -- which has a number of components, both in terms of entities and figures, both within Croatia and in relation to Serbia. This witness has just a lot of detail about those events because of his rather unique position as the president of the Serb region within Croatia. So I -- it may very well be that we will able to get through his evidence more quickly and we will try to. I would like to. But this is one witness where -- and obviously he's much longer than all the other witnesses. And this is one witness where that may end up being appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. What about Witness MM-14? I see he's introducing exhibits, and can't be he added to the 92 bis witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, that's something I could certainly discuss with Defence counsel. This witness will be introducing a large number of documents that were obtained by the OTP and that relate directly to the structure of the police within the SAO Krajina or the Serb entity within Croatia. In many ways goes to the heart of the matter because, of course, this Accused was in charge, in command, of that police so the structure of the police force under his command within the various municipalities within the SAO Krajina will be a critical, important component of this case so it may be important to have this witness come before the Chamber and testify. I would note that it's not a particularly long witness and it may be even shorter than the eight hours that we have predicted. But I will take the Court's suggestion and see with Defence counsel if there is some -- if Defence counsel would agree and perhaps there is some way that this evidence could be put in through -- in written form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber is -- to the Defence witness. May you please perhaps consider doing the same with respect to MM-16, MM-17, MM-18, MM-28, MM-64, and MM-74. If the Prosecution can try to reach an agreement with the Defence to introduce 92 bis evidence for those witnesses, even if they are called for cross-examination possible re-examination, that would be fine, but at least we could curtail the evidence-in-chief part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Certainly I will undertake to do that. I think -- just forecasting I think that it should be -- I would predict that we could reach agreement with respect to 16, 17, and 18, perhaps also with respect to 28 and 74. 64 may be one that would be more difficult to reach agreement on but I will undertake to discuss with Defence counsel all of those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber would be grateful for whatever agreement you can reach. Thank you so much. One item which wasn't an outstanding issue but which came to light is the question of scheduling of the case. Looking at the Court calendar, it appears that two more dates have been allocated to this case, namely the 30th and 31st of March. Would the Prosecution have any objection to sitting on those days?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, not at all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milovancevic, would the Defence be inclined to sit on those two days, the 30th and 31st of March?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. That disposes of the outstanding issues. We can now move on to the opening statements. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. May it please the Court. In the late 1980s, the former Yugoslavia, then known as the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or SFRY composed of six republics and two autonomous provinces, began to break apart. Some of its republics, in particular the republics of Slovenia and Croatia, began to push for independence. However, a group of Serb leaders within the former Yugoslavia, including the Accused Milan Martic, embraced a very different conception, a conception not of autonomous or independent republics but, rather, a conception of a single Serb state, a state for all Serbs, that would cut across the borders of the republics to unite all the areas in the former Yugoslavia where Serbs were in the majority, where they constituted a significant proportion of the population, or where they had a historic claim. The Serb leaders who embraced this conception sought specifically to carve out the Serb areas from the republics of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, in order to join them together with Serbia and Montenegro to create a single Serb state. This goal of a single Serb state was referred to by various names. Greater Serbia, enlarged Serbia, or a state for all Serbs. This case is about war crimes and crimes against humanity that were committed by the Accused, Milan Martic, as he and others tried to implement this conception and create a separate Serb state within Croatia that would become part of this state for all Serbs. The planned area of this state included what's known as the so-called Serb autonomous region of Krajina in Croatia, an area along the Croatian border with Bosnia and Herzegovina with Knin being its largest town. If we can switch to the Sanction on the computer and I would advise the Chamber to press on the computer evidence button, we are showing now a map of Croatia, and we can see the border that runs on the right side there, on either side -- is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are not there. Now we are there. We are with you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we just start with the map again?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. I'm showing -- there is a map of Croatia and you can see on the right side, on either side of the red arrow, the border with Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it's along that border -- we seem -- has the Court lost it on the computer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It lost us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I don't know if this is a problem in the AV booth or -- has it come back?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not on our screen. Okay, there it is. Okay. I'll try this again. This is a map of Croatia, and we can see the border with Bosnia and Herzegovina on either side of that red arrow and that is -- it is along the border that is the Krajina region of Croatia and the red arrow, which we'll zoom in on, points to Knin. This map and others will be provided to the Chamber and entered into evidence in due course. Now, while the Serbs constituted a minority population in Croatia as a whole, in the Krajina region of Croatia, they represented the majority. On the next map that I will show, we can see the different ethnic groups within Croatia in 1991. This is based on the 1991 census. And you can see along the border in the kind of pinkish colour, Mr. Black will draw a circle around it, the pinkish colour represents the predominantly Serb area, and that is the Krajina region in Croatia, whereas the blue colour in the rest of -- in other areas, I should say, of Croatia, represents the majority Croat areas. The case against this Accused is at bottom simple and straightforward. The evidence will show that the Accused and others had a common criminal purpose which was successfully achieved for a number of years, to rid this planned Serb state in Croatia of the Croat and other non-Serb population that resided there. They sought to create this homogeneous Serb state through a campaign of persecutions, often referred to as ethnic cleansing. Croat and other non-Serb civilians became the enemy. In the areas of the planned Serb state where they existed, Croats and other non-Serbs were targeted with discriminatory measures, restriction of movement, forcible removal, imprisonment, torture, and murder, in an effort to drive them away. Their properties were looted and destroyed so that they would never have a home to return to again. In this opening statement, I will provide an overview of the evidence that the Prosecution expects to prove in this case. I will not review all of the evidence, nor will I attempt to touch on all aspects of the charges against this Accused. That has been done in our various written filings. The purpose of this opening statement is simply to provide a road map of the case to the Chamber. During this opening I will also show some exhibits, including some video clips, all of which we expect to be entered into evidence during trial. The story of this case begins in January of 1990. By this time, Serb leaders and the media, including this Accused, were already taking the first steps towards ethnic conflict and ethnic separation, portraying the majority Croat population in Croatia as a threat, a danger, to the Serb minority population in Croatia thereby instilling fear in the Serb population. It is often fear, of course, that allows one ethnic group to consider another ethnic group, neighbours in this case, as the enemy. Now, there is no doubt that on the other side, there were ethnically based incidents perpetrated by certain Croats against Serbs. In addition, there was at times, an insensitivity on the parliament of Croat leaders to the concerns of the Serb population, particularly when these leaders resurrected various symbols from Croatia's past that the Serb population had come to associate with the Croatian fascist regime from World War II. Perhaps here, right at the outset, it is important to state clearly the Prosecution's view that the conflict in Croatia, like virtually any conflict, was not strictly one-sided. Certain events on the Croat side, no doubt contributed at times to the rising tensions and ethnic conflict. However, as a matter of law and a matter of fact, nothing that occurred on the Croat side at any time during this story justified the crimes charged in this indictment. The evidence will show that Serb leaders, including this Accused, exploited the tensions and fanned the flames of fear among the Serb population, claiming even that the Serb population was threatened with imminent genocide at the hands of the Croat majority. These Serb leaders fostered a feeling of fear among the Serb population in order to create support for a separate, homogeneous Serb state. In February of 1990, Serbs in Croatia founded a political party to represent their interests. The Serbian Democratic Party, known as the SDS. The platform of the SDS recited all of the problems faced by Serbs in Croatia and it evoked the threat of genocide. In addition the platform stated, and I quote, "We shall strive for an administrative division of Croatia into regions and municipalities which would reflect more appropriately the ethnic structure of the area in which we live." In other words, redraw the regional and municipality lines that existed in Croatia along ethnic boundaries. The SDS party further advocated autonomy for territories within Croatia with, and again I quote, "A special ethnic composition." So from the very beginning, the SDS embraced both fear, evoking the threat of genocide, and ethnic separation. In 1990 the Accused, Milan Martic, was a police inspector in Knin in Croatia, in the heart of the predominantly Serb area of Croatia. A word about structure and terminology here. Within the republics of the former Yugoslavia, the police, which unlike the army of the former Yugoslavia, was organised on the republic level, performed two functions, ordinary police functions to preserve civil order and state security functions. In 1990, the police force in Croatia was ethnically mixed, comprised of both Croat and Serb officers. The police fell under the Ministry of the Interior and both the police and the Ministry of Interior are often referred to as the MUP or the M-U-P. So we will hear references to the MUP generally, to MUP officers, to MUP stations. At times, there will also be references to the SUP or the S-U-P. That simply refers to a regional office of the M-U-P or MUP. In this regard, we will sometimes hear references to a SUP office or SUP officers. Going back to the story, in early 1990, as a police inspector in Knin, the Accused, Milan Martic, aligned himself with the founder of the SDS, Jovan Raskovic, and began to promote ethnic separation and the fear of genocide at the hand of the Croats. Martic at this time began to organise the Serb policemen as a separate force within the Croatian police. In an interview in 1994, the Accused, Milan Martic, speaking about this time, said, "That at that time I was working on awakening the patriotic consciousness with the Serbs, telling that Croatia was preparing another genocide against Serbs." Let's turn back to the development of the Serb political structures in Croatia. As I said, in January of 1990, the Serb political party, the SDS, was founded. In April and May of 1990, the first multi-party elections were held in Croatia. The SDS party won a majority in four municipalities which are shown on a map on the Sanction. Again, if you press computer evidence that's the best way to see the items on the Sanction. You can see the four municipalities that would be at the core of the intended Serbian entity in the Krajina of Croatia: Knin, Gracac, Benkovac, and Donji Lapac. The president of the SDS party -- they are shaded in green on the map. The president of the SDS party in the Knin municipality, and the president of the Knin municipality itself, was a man by the name of Milan Babic, an important figure in this story who would, during 1990 and 1991, become the highest political leader of the separate Serb political entity in the Croatian Krajina, which was first known as the Serbian autonomous district of Krajina, or SAO Krajina, and later known as the Republic of Serbian Krajina or RSK after it joined with two other Serbian autonomous districts in Croatia. Babic was therefore the political counterpart to Milan Martic. Babic became the president of the planned Serb state in the Croatian Krajina while Martic became the commander of its armed forces. Martic and his followers within the police rejected the new Croatian police uniform which Martic said was a symbol of the Croatian fascist state of World War II. And in July of 1990, he and a mob of unruly Serb policemen faced down the Croatian interior minister, who was Martic's ultimate superior in the government, and who had come to Knin with his aids in order to try to calm the growing unrest. The Accused later bragged about how much he had scared the interior minister and his aides on this occasion and about how these men required Martic's protection in order to leave Knin safely. Now, as Martic began to organise the Serb policemen in the Krajina, he did not act alone. Rather, he had critical help and support from the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia or what's called the MUP of Serbia. This help and support came through two of its most important figures, Jovica Stanisic and Frenki Simatovic, both leaders within the Serbian MUP, both indicted in a separate case at this Tribunal, for many of the same dilemmas are charged against this Accused. Stanisic and Simatovic, who themselves were under the control of Slobodan Milosevic in Serbia, provided essential support to Martic and the Serb police in the Croatian Krajina, in the form of direction, financial support, and weapons. Throughout the time period of this case, Martic, his associates in the Serbian MUP, and Milosevic will sometimes be described as a parallel structure. While Martic held positions and functioned within the local Serb political police and military structure in the Croatian Krajina, he also had loyalties and was responsive to Serb leaders in Serbia who shared his goal of a separate state for all Serbs. Over time, the Accused Martic's loyalty to those Serb leaders outside of the Croatian Krajina became stronger than ties he had to the political figures within the Krajina, including Milan Babic. Also, as we shall see, Martic eventually received the support not just of the Serbian MUP and of Serb political figures in Serbia but also of the Yugoslav army, which was known as the JNA, which in August of 1991 ended its official stance of neutrality in the conflict and entered the war in Croatia on the side of Serb forces. But we are getting a little ahead of the story. Let's go back to 1990 for a moment where we see the two intertwined developments that are central to this case. First, as we have seen, the Serbs in Croatia began organising themselves in the Krajina into a separate political and geographic structure. This movement which started with the aspirations of the SDS, the Serb political party, at the beginning of 1990, quickly led to the creation of various political structures within the Krajina that were meant to serve as a separate government for Serbs in Croatia. By the end of 1990, less than a year later, Serbs in the Croatian Krajina had in fact created a separate political and geographic structure which was comprised of Serb municipalities and villages in the Krajina. This entity would be in existence in one form or another until August of 1995. But it was never recognised as a separate state by the international community. For this reason, we will hear references to the so-called Serbian autonomous district of Krajina or SAO Krajina, and the so-called Republic of Serbian Krajina, or RSK, which, as I mentioned earlier, was created by combining the SAO Krajina with two other Serbian autonomous districts in Croatia, the SAO Western Slavonia and the SAO Eastern Slavonia Baranja and Western Srem. More on that later. The second development that occurred in 1990 -- the first development is the political development -- the second development that occurred in 1990 was the creation, under the direction of Milan Martic, the Accused, of a separate Serb police force in the Croatian Krajina that would act as the muscle and the armed forces of the Serb political and geographic structure. By the end of 1990, this force was also firmly in place and under the Accused's -- under the command of the Accused, Milan Martic. The force was known by various names, such as Martic's Police, Martic's Milicija, the Marticevci, meaning Martic's men, or the SAO Krajina Milicija. This force was comprised of Serb police loyal to Martic as well as other Serbs in the Krajina who took up arms and supported Martic. Going back to the political development in the SAO Krajina in 1990, let's take a moment to trace the steps in 1990 that led to the creation of a separate Serb political structure in the Croatian Krajina. I talked about the elections where the SDS won a majority in four municipalities. In June of 1990, Milan Babic and others established what they called the association of Serbian municipalities much northern Dalmatia and Lika, which was the first formal step towards creating a separate Serb political and geographic entity. Northern -- northern Dalmatia and Lika refer to regions within Croatia and as shown on the map now being shown on the Sanction, the association of Serbian municipalities of northern Dalmatia and Lika included the municipalities of Knin, Benkovac, Gracac and Donji Lapac, the four municipalities where the SDS had won the majority, plus the municipalities of Obrovac and Korenica. In July of 1990, a Serbian assembly was held in the town of Serb, a town which is within the municipality of Donji Lapac and which is going to be shown on the map that is on the Sanction now, by zooming in on that area of Croatia, and we can see Knin and just to the north of Knin being indicated by the red arrow is the town of Srb where the Serbian assembly was held in July of 1990. This assembly was attended by approximately 100.000 Serbs, mostly Croatian Serbs, including members of the SDS, presidents of Serb municipalities, Serbian deputies in the parliament of the Republic of Croatia, and representatives of the Serbian Orthodox Church. Here I'm going to show you -- this is a -- some photos of the assembly, and the crowd, the enormous crowd, is visible, and the next photo is a photo of Milan Babic addressing the crowd in Srb. The assembly adopted what was called a declaration on the sovereignty and autonomy of the Serbian people, which took a number of further steps towards the creation of a separate Serb state in Croatia. It declared that the Serbian people constituted a sovereign nation within Croatia and it established both a Serbian assembly as a representative of the Serbian people, and a Serbian national council to act as the executive body. Finally the declaration stated that if Croatia remained within Yugoslavia, then the Serbs in Croatia would demand cultural autonomy. But if Yugoslavia became a confederation of independent republics, then the Serbs would demand both political and territorial autonomy. These were further steps towards defining a separate Serb state within Croatia. When the Serbian national council next met in August of 1990, it called for a referendum to be held among Serbs on the question of -- on the question of autonomy for Serbs in Croatia. This was a referendum that was held among Serbs. And 99.7 per cent of those who voted supported autonomy. But the greater significance of this referendum which occurred in August of 1990 lies elsewhere. This referendum brought together in a dramatic fashion the two strands that were developing at this time that I have referred to, the separate Serb political and geographic entity that was being established by Milan Babic and the other Serb leaders and the Serb police force under the control of the Accused, Milan Martic. This occurred because, on the 17th of August 1990, the Croatian government declared the referendum within the Serb communities to be illegal and the Croatian police began to take steps to interfere with the referendum. The Serb police under Martic's command, reacted, seizing reserve police weapons and distributing them to Serbs. As Martic himself later said in an interview, "We took care not to give militia weapons to Croats. I personally ordered the militia to take all the long weapons with them and to safeguard the rest of the arms day and night." The Serbs also erected blockades in Knin and elsewhere under Martic's command in order to stop the Croatian authorities from entering the area in what became known as the "log revolution," so named because of the logs that were sometimes used in the blockades. This event cemented Martic's role as leader of the Serb police in Croatia and it showed the willingness of the Serb police under Martic's command to take up arms, to fight for the separate Serb political and geographic state that was being created. By this time, Martic no longer considered him self to be under the authority of the Croatian government at all. Watch him speaking to a reporter a few weeks after the beginning of the log revolution and listen to what he says about the Croatian government. The video will be played on the Sanction and a transcript of what is being said in English will appear below the video and has been synchronised to play in time with the video. If that could be --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In August of 1990, at this time, at the time of the log revolution, at the time Martic cemented his control over the Martic's Police, Martic sought even more control from Serbia. He sent a message to leaders of Serbia, including Slobodan Milosevic, that the Serbs in Croatia needed either more weapons or the support of the army of Yugoslavia, the JNA. As I mentioned earlier, the JNA at this time claimed officially at least, to be taking a neutral stance between the two sides of the conflict in Croatia and purported to intervene only to act as a buffer between the two sides. But after August of 1990, that is during the remainder of 1990 and the first half of 1991, Martic and his police sought to draw the JNA into the conflict on the sides of the Serbs by provoking clashes with the Croatian government. So let's move ahead now to the end of 1990. In December, there was a further formalisation of the separate Serb political structure in Croatia. The association of municipalities of northern Dalmatia and Lika was transformed into an entity called the Serbian autonomous district of Krajina or SAO Krajina, which included all the municipalities that had been included in the association of municipalities of northern Dalmatia and Lika as well as other Serb municipalities and villages in the Krajina area that wished to join. This was the entity in existence in the fall of 1991 during many of the crimes charged in this indictment. On the screen is a map of the municipalities and areas that were part of the so-called SAO Krajina by April of 1991, and they are coloured in green on this map. The area of the SAO Krajina increased in part through fighting and conflict, by the end of 1991, and this map shows the larger area that was under the control of the SAO Krajina by the end of 1991. And Mr. Black is drawing in red the area of the SAO Krajina by the -- at the end of 1991. The other areas are other SAOs, Serbian autonomous districts that I will refer to later. But the area in red is the SAO Krajina. The SAO Krajina which was created in December of 1990, had both an assembly and an executive council. Milan Babic became the president of the executive council of the SAO Krajina, while on January 4th of 1991, Milan Martic was appointed to the position of secretary of the interior of the SAO Krajina, with full control of Martic's Police. On April 1st 1991, the executive council of the SAO Krajina passed a decision joining the SAO Krajina to the Republic of Serbia, a further step towards joining together the Serb areas of the former Yugoslavia into a single Serb state. The executive council also declared that the constitution and the laws of Serbia and of Yugoslavia would apply in the SAO Krajina instead of the laws of the Republic of Croatia. In May of 1991, another referendum was held in the Serb areas of Croatia on the question of whether the SAO Krajina should stay with Serbia and Montenegro within Yugoslavia. Again, this was held in the Serb areas in the SAO Krajina and the referendum was approved by 99.8 per cent of those voting. At the same time, the Republic of Croatia was itself moving towards independence from the former Yugoslavia. In May of 1991, a referendum on the question of independence was held in Croatia but it was boycotted by the SAO Krajina. It passed by 94 per cent of those voting. On June 25th of 1991, Croatia declared independence. However, in agreement with the European Community, Croatia agreed to suspend implementation of its independence until October of 1991. Within the SAO Krajina, Martic's position became further defined, and on May 29th of 1991, he was elected by the assembly to be the Minister of Defence of the SAO Krajina, while the position of interior minister was given to another, more moderate individual. Martic resisted this move, however, and one month later he re-assumed his position as interior minister. During this entire time when he was defence minister and then when he re-assumed the position as interior minister the Accused Milan Martic retained full control over Martic's Police or the SAO Krajina Police. Also at this time something of a rivalry developed between the two main Serb leaders in the Croatian Krajina, Milan Babic and Milan Martic. While the two men shared many of the same goals for the Serbs in Croatia, they nonetheless competed for power. However, the evidence will show that Babic never seriously challenged Martic's hold over the armed Serb formations in Croatia and Babic's role remained almost entirely a political one. In the summer of 1991, Babic did try to assert control over the Serb elements of the Territorial Defence forces in the Krajina. Now, a word of explanation here about the function and role of the Territorial Defence within the former Yugoslavia. In addition to the army, the JNA, there also existed what was called a Territorial Defence, often referred to as the TO, which existed more on the local level within the republics. The Territorial Defence was generally staffed by older individuals and was often commanded by officers who were retired from the JNA. During peace time, the Territorial Defence fell under the command of the president of the republic, while during wartime it was under the command of the army, the JNA. In Croatia, therefore, the Territorial Defence would fall under the control of the Croatian government except during wartime when it would pass to the JNA. Now, when the SAO Krajina came into existence in Croatia, there was an effort to put the Territorial Defence units that existed within the SAO Krajina under Serb control. And, as I said earlier, in the summer of 1991, Milan Babic, as president of the SAO Krajina, sought to take control of these Serb territorial units within the SAO Krajina and he tried to form a command structure to run them. However, this effort was never successful. First of all, those Serbs who wanted to take up arms in the SAO Krajina for the most part either joined the JNA or Martic's Police, and so in many areas in the SAO Krajina, the so-called Territorial Defence existed on paper only and had no personnel. Second, Martic himself sought to assert control over the Territorial Defence. In August of 1991, Babic was pressured by Milosevic to appoint Martic as the deputy commander of the Territorial Defence in the SAO Krajina and moreover, certain units of the Territorial Defence were loyal only to Martic. The evidence will show that at the end of the day, Martic had more control over the Territorial Defence than Babic did. Moreover, during actual military operations, such as those that occurred during the fall months of 1991, the Territorial Defence units were subordinated to the army, to the JNA, and as we will see in a moment, in -- by August of 1991, on the eve of the war, the JNA and Martic's police were fully aligned. Now, earlier I said that in the latter months of 1990 and the first half of 1991, Martic and his police sought to provoke clashes with the Croatian authorities in order to draw the JNA into the conflict on the side of the Serbs. In March of 1991, for example, Martic's Police took over Plitvice national park. The location of that is being shown on the Sanction. Plitvice national park is an important tourist attraction in the municipality of Korenica, one of the municipalities that had joined the SAO Krajina. And Mr. Black will zoom in on that. There it is on the map, in the northern part of Korenica. Fighting broke out between the Croatian MUP -- this again in March of 1991 -- fighting broke out between the Croatian MUP and Martic's police and one policeman from each side was killed. The JNA then entered the conflict and imposed a cease-fire. Other similar clashes occurred during the early months of 1991. In addition, Croatian civilians began to come under attack within the SAO Krajina. In April of 1991, a Croatian restaurant near Knin was destroyed by an explosive. Martic was in charge, of course, of the police in the SAO Krajina but the news report that we are about to show you captured his attitude towards attacks on Croat civilians at this time. And we will play that report on the Sanction, and again, the transcript of what's being said will appear beneath the video and will be synchronised, if that could be played now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: According to this news report, Martic said that since the police was focused on defending the borders of the SAO Krajina, they had no time to investigate crimes committed against Croat civilians. The real turning point in the conflict occurred, however, in August of 1991. As is visible on the map that is being shown now on the Sanction, Kijevo, which will be pointed out by a red arrow, is a village that lies just to the south of Knin. At that time, Kijevo was a Croatian village that lay between Knin to the north and several Serb villages to the south. The Accused, Milan Martic, in August of 1991, wanted to take control of this village and he issued an ultimatum to the Croatian authorities to abandon the police station in Kijevo, warning the civilian population of an attack if this was not done. Then, the significant part of this event occurred. The JNA abandoned its official policy of neutrality and openly entered the conflict on the side of the Serbs. After Martic's ultimatum expired, JNA forces, elements of Martic's police, and the local Serb Territorial Defence unit all under the unified command of the JNA, attacked, took control of and cleansed Kijevo of all Croats living there. In an interview in 1994, the Accused, Milan Martic, spoke very openly about the attack on Kijevo, the cooperation between his forces and the JNA, and Milan Babic's opposition to this attack. Martic said, "Babic thought the question of Kijevo could be solved in a different way. He even issued a statement that Kijevo shouldn't be attacked. However, my opinion was stronger, and in coordination with the JNA, we did it my way. We gave the infantry, police and civilian, and the logistics was provided by the JNA. We conquered Kijevo." Martic also said in the interview, "To be honest, we seem to be superior to the Croatians and they were running away. We didn't care about the victims. We wanted to liberate our blocked villages. Of course, there were a few burnt houses. That's the way it goes in these actions with artillery. We thought it wouldn't last long, and we were right. Colonel Mladic was there as well, and he was pleased. It was the first JNA success. They weren't very successful in Slovenia and Croatia before this. It was his personal success, and I was happy for him, and us, for doing the job well." Colonel Ratko Mladic, who was then the Chief of Staff of the JNA 9th Corps in Knin himself spoke about the operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you? Has the quote not ended? Are you still quoting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the quote has ended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: For doing the job well, at the end of well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's not closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll make sure to indicate that on future quotations, Your Honour. Colonel Ratko Mladic, who was then the Chief of Staff of the JNA 9th Corps in Knin himself spoke about the operation in Kijevo during a speech at the 16th session of the Assembly of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina held on the 12th of May 1992 in Banja Luka. The accused Milan Martic was present for this speech. Mladic said, "The Knin corps was successful because under a single command in the zone of the corps, were the JNA, the TO, and Martic's Police. Isn't that right, Martic? And because he and I -- I call him and say, "Given me 40 policemen here at Kijevo, and you took part in the fighting, isn't that right, Milan? And we did what we had planned." General Veljko Kadijevic, who was federal secretary of the JNA later wrote in a book called "My View of the Break-up," that from the end of summer of 1991 the task of the JNA was to, "Protect the Serb people in Croatia in such a way that all regions with a majority Serb population would be completely freed from the presence of the Croatian army and the Croatian authorities." He further explained that this was accomplished in, "Full coordination with Serb insurgents in the Serbian Krajina." From August of 1991 on, as charged in this indictment, the JNA, the Accused, Milan Martic, and his police, Serb Territorial Defence units, and some Serb volunteer units, attacked Croat villages in the SAO Krajina and on its borders, engaging in a coordinated campaign of persecutions of Croat and other non-Serb civilians. The purpose was to cleanse the intended Serbian state of non-Serbs. The attacks were often preceded by shelling and blockades. Typically the attack itself was led by the JNA with the other Serb forces, including Martic's Police coming in afterwards to ethnically cleanse the village. In connection with these attacks, Croat and other non-Serb civilians were forcibly removed from their villages, arbitrarily arrested, detained, beaten, tortured and murdered. Cultural and sacred sites of non-Serbs, as well as private property belonging to non-Serbs were intentionally destroyed and plundered. These attacks were particularly intense from August of 1991 until January of 1992, at which time a cease-fire was implemented. The persecutory campaign continued, however, through 1995 and, as a result of this campaign of ethnic cleansing, nearly the entire non-Serb population of the SAO Krajina was either removed or was killed. I will not describe in detail all of the attacks that occurred during this campaign of persecutions. I will just touch on a few. Dubica, Bacin, and Cerovljani are villages which are on the border between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Croatian municipality of Kostajnica, and it's being shown on the Sanction now where those villages are located in Croatia. In 1991, these villages had mixed populations, though with a majority of Croats. Before September of 1991, there were armed clashes between Serb forces and Croatian forces, but in September of 1991, the Croatian forces withdrew and the Serb forces, in particular Martic's Police and his Serb Territorial Defence unit, took control of the villages. Martic's Police establish a police station in Dubica, one of these villages. In September of 1991, the Serb forces arrested a number of Croat civilians in these villages and detained them. The detainees were used as human shields and as mine detectors when Serb forces were looting houses. The detainees were beaten and abused, and some were ordered to carry the bodies of other dead detainees. Houses belonging to Croats in these villages were burned. On October 20th of 1991, these Serb forces, including, in particular, elements of Martic's Police rounded up some 53 elderly civilians from Dubica and took them to a fire station. If you look at the ages of these civilians on Annex I of the indictment, you will see that many were more than 60 or 70 years old. One woman was 90. Ten of these civilians were released, apparently because of connections that they had to Serbs. But the remaining 43 were executed the following day along with a number of elderly civilians from Bacin and Cerovljani. Saborsko is a village located near Plitvice in the Ogulin municipality and it is being shown on the Sanction now. In August of 1991, it was a large village inhabited almost entirely by Croats. Nearby, were the villages much Poljanak, Lipovaca, and Vukovici, but these villages were surrounded by Serb-controlled villages. Starting in August of 1991, Serb forces began shelling Saborsko, driving away many of its non-Serb civilians. In the following months, Martic's Police and other Serb forces arrested Croat men from Saborsko and the other Croat villages. These men were detained and in many cases brutally beaten. In late October and early November, Poljanak, Lipovaca, and Vukovici, and, finally, Saborsko were all attacked by Serb forces. Croat civilians were deliberately and intentionally massacred during these attacks. In Vukovici, for example, Serb forces removed eight civilians from a house, including some who were elderly and others who were female, lined them up against the house and simply executed them. Then they went into the house and executed a man who was too sick to leave his bed. On November 12th of 1991, Serb forces mounted a full-scale attack on Saborsko itself. Saborsko was first attacked by JNA planes dropping bombs and then by Serb soldiers who pulled civilians from basements where they had taken shelter, separated the men from the women, and executed some 20 men. All of the inhabitants of Saborsko were driven from the village and all of the houses in the village and the Catholic church were then burned to the ground. Skabrnja and Nadin are a pair of villages in the part of the Zadar municipality that borders the municipality of Benkovac. This part of the Zadar municipality broke off and joined with the SAO Krajina. They were ethnically mixed villages but they were strategically important because they were situated on a road linking Zadar with Benkovac. Serb forces began to shell Skabrnja and Nadin in September of 1991 driving away many of the civilian residents. On November 18th and 19th, Skabrnja and Nadin were attacked by the JNA, Martic's Police, and the Benkovac local Serb Territorial Defence unit. As in Saborsko civilians were pulled out of cellars where they had hidden and were summarily executed. In all some 38 civilians were executed in Skabrnja and another seven in Nadin. Others were arrested and detained during the attack. In the following months, another 26 civilians were killed by Serb forces in and around Skabrnja. The result of these attacks? These previously mixed villages were ethnically cleansed of their non-Serb inhabitants. These are just some of the attacks by Serb forces on Croat villages and civilians that occurred during the fall months of 1991. These and others will be proven during trial. I've touched on these only to show the pattern of the ethnic cleansing campaign. Villages with Croat populations were first put under siege, blockaded, and then often shelled. Individual Croats were arrested and detained. The villages were then attacked and the remaining Croat civilians were either driven out, arrested, or murdered. The Croat parts of the villages were destroyed to ensure that the Croat civilians could not return. All of this done by a combination of Serb forces working together, the JNA, Martic's Police, and local Serb Territorial Defence units. During this time, Milan Martic was unquestionably in command of Martic's Police and was therefore the most important commander of local Serb forces within the Croatian Krajina itself, and Milan Babic was the highest political leader of the Serbs in the Krajina. The Accused Martic worked together with other Serb leaders in Croatia and Serbia and with other Serb commanders of Serb forces toward the common goal of achieving an ethnically homogeneous Serb state in Croatia. Your Honours, I pause because I'm not sure when Your Honours wish to take a break. Now would be an appropriate time for me if that's--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It appears this is an appropriate time. I think this is the time we can take the break. We will take an adjournment and we will come back at ten to four. Court is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. At the end of November of 1991, a cease-fire in Croatia was negotiated between Slobodan Milosevic, Franjo Tudjman, and General Kadijevic of the JNA, under the auspices of Cyrus Vance, who was then acting as a United Nations special envoy. It is significant, of course, that this cease-fire was negotiated by Milosevic, further evidence of his connection to the Serb forces in Croatia. The negotiated agreement which are became known as the Vance Plan was formally signed at the beginning of January 1992 and established what were called United Nations Protected Areas, known as UNPAs in Croatia that were monitored by UN peacekeeping forces. The agreement contemplated the withdrawal of the JNA, the lifting of the blockade of JNA barracks, and the demilitarisation of Serb forces in Croatia. The goal of demilitarisation, however, was circumvented when Serb forces in Croatia simply renamed themselves as police units. They were called special police units or the PJM, and they retained their heavy weapons, including weapons and resources left by the withdrawing JNA. Now, initially, Milan Martic opposed the Vance Plan but then he was persuaded to accept it. Milan Babic, however, remained opposed to the Vance Plan, fearing that a JNA withdrawal from Croatia would leave the Serbs there unprotected. This stance by Babic put him on an open collision course with Slobodan Milosevic, who had negotiated and who supported the plan. A collision course that would cost Milan Babic his position. In December of 1991, the SAO Krajina transformed itself one more time and became the Republic of Serbian Krajina or RSK. Initially, Milan Babic was the president of the RSK and Milan Martic continued as the interior minister in charge of all police forces. In February of 1992, two other Serb areas in Croatia that had organised themselves as Serb autonomous districts, the area of Western Slavonia and the area of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem joined the RSK. Now, the map being shown now shows the areas that fell under the control of the RSK after February of 1992. We are familiar with the area that was the Krajina. The next area to the right is the SAO Western Slavonia. And then the final area to the right bordering on Serbia is the area of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. These areas combined formed the RSK. Now, in February of 1992, at the time that these areas joined together to become the RSK, Milan Babic was voted out as the president of the RSK and was replaced by Goran Hadzic. This was in part because of Babic's opposition to the Vance Plan. Milan Martic, however, continued as the minister of the interior of the RSK. Now, let's pause here for a moment to talk about Milan Babic who in this story has just lost his job as president of the RSK. As I said, during 1990 and 1991, Milan Babic was the highest political leader of the Serbs in the Croatian Krajina. While he competed with Milan Martic for control of the local Serb Territorial Defence forces in the SAO Krajina, the evidence will show that he never exercised effective control of these forces, and that Milan Martic was in fact the principal commander of these forces -- of local Serb forces within the SAO Krajina. Nonetheless, in his political role, Milan Babic provided critical support to the campaign of persecutions against Croat and other non-Serb civilians in the SAO Krajina from August of 1991 until February of 1992. For his role in these events, Milan Babic pled guilty at this Tribunal on January 22nd 2004, to being a co-perpetrator of a joint criminal enterprise that committed the crime of persecutions, a crime against humanity, and the same crime that is charged in count 1 of the indictment against this Accused, Milan Martic. Before pleading guilty, Milan Babic cooperated with the Office of the Prosecutor and he testified in the ongoing trial against Slobodan Milosevic. Following his guilty plea, Milan Babic received a sentence of 13 years imprisonment which he is now serving. Let's turn back now to the events in February of 1992. As I said, Milan Martic continued as the Minister of the interior of the RSK in command of the police. During 1992, the RSK organised a Territorial Defence which then became an army which was known as the SVK. The SVK was the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. The special police units under Martic's command were formally incorporated into the military structure of the RSK. From 1992, until 1995, Serb forces in the RSK, including Martic's Police, continued to persecute the few remaining non-Serbs within the RSK. Now, at the end of 1993, a presidential election was held in the so-called RSK. And guess who ran in that election? Milan Babic against Milan Martic. Martic received considerable and critical support from Slobodan Milosevic, and in the second round of voting in 1994, Martic was elected the president of the RSK. Now, let's watch a video of Martic during this campaign for president and let's hear how he talked about his relationship with Milosevic at this time, if the Sanction could be played.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: As it is clear from this video clip, Milan Martic in the presidential campaign continued to advocate a single state for all Serbs and he made clear his allegiance to Serb leaders outside of Croatia, namely Slobodan Milosevic and Radovan Karadzic, the Bosnian Serb leader. He pledged to pass the baton, if he were elected, to our all-Serbian leader, Slobodan Milosevic. Now, when he became president of the RSK, Milan Martic became commander of all the military forces of the RSK. During 1994 and 1995, the international community sought to resolve the status of the RSK within Croatia in what became known as the Z-4 process. Z being a reference to Zagreb and 4 a reference to the four international entities that participated in the negotiations, the United States, Russia, the United Nations, and the European Union. The difficulty was that the Serb leaders in Croatia continued to seek independence for the RSK while the Croatian government continued to be resistant to a separate Serb state on Croatian territory. In early 1995, the Z-4 process resulted in a draft agreement that would have granted the RSK considerable autonomy. Milan Martic, however, rejected this plan. The representative of the United States during the Z-4 process was the United States ambassador to Croatia, Peter Galbraith. Ambassador Galbraith met with Milan Martic in late 1994 at which time Martic suggested that in the event of military action by the Croatian government, the RSK would launch a rocket attack on Zagreb. This is in 1994, this discussion takes place. Ambassador Galbraith told Milan Martic in no uncertain terms that a rocket attack on Zagreb would constitute a crime. In 1995, when the Z-4 process stalled, the Croatian government did in fact initiate military action against the RSK, attacking first the area of Western Slavonia on May 1st 1995 in what was known as Operation Flash. In reaction to this attack on Western Slavonia, despite having been explicitly warned by Ambassador Galbraith that it would constitute a crime, Milan Martic ordered the firing of 12 Orkan rockets on the city of Zagreb and other areas on May 2nd and May 3rd. These rockets were fitted with cluster bomb warheads which, the evidence will show, are designed to explode in the air, spraying thousands of small ball bearings which are designed to kill people or do damage to lightly armoured vehicles. These rockets hit residential and commercial areas of Zagreb and killed five civilians and wounded 146 others on the first day, and on the second day, killed two more civilians and wounded 48 more. On the Sanction is a map showing the areas of impact of the rockets in Zagreb. The five rockets in the upper left of this map hit right in downtown Zagreb. Now, let's listen to the Accused, Milan Martic, taking responsibility for these rocket attacks on the radio within a day of the attacks being launched. I warn you that the sound quality as it's played through the Sanction system of this radio transmission is a little bit difficult at times to hear. There is a little bit of interference, but the transcript will be played on the Sanction as the radio transmission is played. If we could play that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: As Milan Martic says in that transmission, "My order to shell Zagreb ensued." Of course, the accused Martic has admitted on numerous occasions, even here at this Tribunal, that he ordered the rocket attack on Zagreb. In this radio statement that we just heard, Martic makes it clear that the attacks were either pure retaliation or a tactic to terrorise the Croats in order to force them to stop their own military attacks or to forgo any future military attacks. Needless to say, neither reason constitutes a legitimate or lawful justification for Martic's murderous attack on the civilian population of Zagreb. Later, Martic tried to claim that the attacks were aimed at military targets. The only arguable military targets, however, within the centre of Zagreb were buildings such as the Ministry of Defence or the Ministry of the Interior or the presidential palace. There were some army barracks but they were located outside the city, no where near where the rockets fell. The cluster bomb rockets used in the attacks are completely useless against buildings such as the ministries of defence and interior as they are designed solely for attacking personnel or lightly armoured vehicles spread out over a large area, and there will be evidence about this at trial. The truth is, Your Honours, Milan Martic intentionally targeted civilians in Zagreb or was aware of the substantial likelihood that his actions would target civilians, and, as Ambassador Galbraith warned, doing so was a crime. Let's watch a few clips, this without transcript, just visual images, of the damage that was inflicted in the areas of Zagreb and the terror that was caused. In watching these clips, it will be obvious that these attacks targeted civilian areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: A little more than two months after these attacks on Zagreb, on July 25th of 1995, Milan Martic was publicly indicted by this Tribunal for these attacks. He remained a fugitive for nearly seven years until he was threatened with arrest by the authorities of Serbia and was therefore forced to surrender to this Tribunal. That is a brief summary of what the evidence will show happened in this case. There are many components to the story and various players. But as I said before, the story is essentially a simple one. The Accused and others conceived of a separate Serb state in the Croatian Krajina to be joined to other Serb areas to create a state for all Serbs. They pursued a common purpose to create such a state and through the commission of crimes they cleansed the planned state of virtually all Croats and other non-Serbs. A word about the evidence that will be used to prove these facts. The evidence presented by the Prosecution will include witnesses who will come to testify before you, written testimony admitted under the Rules of the Tribunal, contemporaneous documents, and public source materials. None of these sources of evidence necessarily has more weight than any others, and it is the nature of these cases and the evidence that some facts will be proven primarily by written statements or documents. Our goal on the Prosecution side during this trial will be always to present a true and accurate picture of what happened in Croatia during the relevant years, to do justice to all of the evidence, and to focus on the role and the responsibility of this Accused for the crimes charged in the indictment. That is our responsibility to this Chamber, to the parties, to the victims and to the world that is watching. Having set forth a summary of the facts, let me just say a few words about the law. I will not try to address all the elements of the crimes charged for they are many; this has already been done in various written filings. But let me just say something about the modes of liability charged in this case. The Accused, Milan Martic, is charged under Article 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute for all of the crimes. The indictment alleges that as commander of Martic's Police and other Serb forces, such as units of the Territorial Defence, and later as president of the RSK in command of all the Serb forces of the RSK, Milan Martic planned, ordered, and instigated or aided and abetted others to commit the campaign of persecutions against the Croat and other non-Serb population, as well as the other specific crimes charged in the indictment, including extermination, murder, imprisonment, torture, inhumane acts, cruel treatment, deportation and forcible transfer, wanton destruction of property and plunder, and unlawful attacks on civilians. It is specifically charged that Martic was a direct perpetrator of the crimes that occurred at the prison in Knin. With respect to all of the crimes charged in the indictment, it is alleged that the Accused intended that the crimes be committed or was aware of the substantial likelihood that his actions would result in their commission. The indictment also alleges that the Accused, Milan Martic, committed all of these crimes through his participation in a joint criminal enterprise, along with other Serb leaders and forces in Croatia, in Croatia and outside Croatia, including Serb leaders and forces from Serbia. The charge is that Milan Martic acted together with these other Serb leaders and entities to accomplish the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise, that is the forcible removal of Croats and other non-Serbs from the territory of the planned Serb state in Croatia through the commission of crimes. Milan Babic you will recall plead guilty to having committed the crimes of persecution through his participation in this same joint criminal enterprise. The evidence will show that Martic worked in close coordination with other members of the joint criminal enterprise including Slobodan Milosevic, Jovica Stanisic, and Frenki Simatovic, and others of the Serbian MUP, the JNA, Milan Babic, and others, in order to accomplish the goals of the joint criminal enterprise. This is not a charge of guilt by association. Milan Martic is not guilty because he associated with the wrong people. Rather, the evidence will show beyond a reasonable doubt that Milan Martic is guilty of the crimes charged in the indictment because he and others had a common purpose to cleanse the Serb territory of Croatia of non-Serbs and undertook actions to achieve this common purpose. This mode of liability is a recognition of the fact that these kinds of crimes are rarely accomplished by one person acting alone or even by a single entity. Rather they can only be accomplished by various entities working together toward a common goal. An individual is guilty and is responsible for the acts of the joint criminal enterprise if it is proven beyond a reasonable doubt that he knowingly and intentionally participated in the joint criminal enterprise and sought to further its criminal aims. The indictment alleges that the crimes charged in the indictment were within the scope of the purpose of the joint criminal enterprise or, in the alternative, that the purpose was the forcible removal of the Croat and other non-Serb population, counts 10 and 11 of the indictment, and the other crimes were a natural and foreseeable consequence of affecting that common purpose. Finally the indictment also charged that the accused Milan Martic as the commander of subordinate forces committing the crimes alleged in the indictment either failed to prevent the commission of the crimes or failed to punish them. The evidence will show that the crimes that were being committed were well known, were repeated, that Milan Martic was aware of them, and that he did nothing to prevent them or to punish them. Your Honours, this brings me to the end of my opening statement. Let me say only in closing that it is our respectful submission that once the evidence is presented to you and it is submitted, it will show beyond a reasonable doubt that the Accused committed the crimes that are at issue in this indictment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milovancevic, you indicated yesterday that Mr. Martic might exercise his right in terms of Rule 84 bis to make an opening statement. Is that still the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Martic has prepared his own opening statement, which should take about 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then, before Mr. Martic makes his statement, the Chamber just will explain a few of his rights to him. Mr. Martic, the statement you are about to make is not a solemn declaration. It is not sworn testimony, in other words. However, its probative value may be looked at, at a later stage, and it might form part of the evidence, depending on what evidence comes out in either corroboration or contradiction of what you may have said. Let me warn you here that you are not forced to make any statement at this stage. It is your right to defend yourself by remaining silent, if you so wish, and if you choose to make a statement, you must do so voluntarily and freely. You have the right not to confess any guilt or to testify against yourself. May I also say that I hope your statement will be kept relevant to the issues before the Court in this matter, and not be intended to make irrelevant statements that have nothing to do with the case. I hope, Mr. Martic, you understand, and if you do, please say so, and you may proceed to make your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand everything. I still wish to make a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, after more than 1.300 days of detention in Scheveningen I have concluded that the indictment against me fed by dubious witnesses has been becoming more and more serious. If I were to trust the other side in these proceedings, at least a little, I would probably end up a nervous wreck. In my madness I would probably tell them I am guilty, do whatever you like. However, I have not reached such a state. God knows during those days when I was one of the leaders of Serbs who were persecuted in Croatia, which had just seceded in Knin and in any other place, all I did was protect every citizen of the Republic of Serbian Krajina regardless of their ethnic or religious affiliations. I protected them from wrongs that might have befallen them in the middle of that war. I have pleaded several times not guilty. Today, after so much time, I have to repeat these same two words: Not guilty. While I read the indictment sometimes I was thinking about giving up the reading of the indictment in which everything with the exception of my first and last names is erroneous, and arbitrary, as I hope the Defence will show. The indictment creates a lot of confusion about both date and time and events and places proving that I was somewhere that I was physically not present and that I did things that I simply didn't do. It was only rarely and with reluctance that I requested my Defence to apply for my provisional release. The reason for this is simple. Until I prove my innocence, there is no freedom that would suit me. I would feel the same here in detention in Scheveningen or enjoying perceived freedom elsewhere. What I want is really freedom. I want the truth and the suffering of the Serbs in the Republic of Krajina in Croatia to be known. That truth matters more to me than my personal freedom or even my life. It is true that I, Milan Martic, former police Minister of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, as well as the last president of that unfortunately temporary state, intend to prove the innocence of my people, of my Krajina people, here before you. They too suffered with me and not because of me, in the war. I will stand here to defend my people from those who took everything from my people and from me personally. I will be defending them from those who should be the ones with the obligation to prove that there was a reason to commit genocide against the Serbian people. These are the conclusions that my defence and I have reached after more than three and a half years of my detention. It is quite apparent that the OTP is not interested in getting at the truth of what happened in the former Yugoslavia. For the OTP, there is no such thing as Yugoslavia, in terms of being a sovereign state back in 1990 and 1991. The OTP does not want to know about real perpetrators or those who gave the orders for crimes to be committed. What they want to do is artificially single out certain events and view them as the truth of what happened in the former Yugoslavia. They have construed a theory about a joint criminal enterprise. According to the indictment I myself played one of the leading roles in this alleged enterprise, aimed at "destroying," as it reads, "all non-Serb population in predominantly Serb territories with the objective of creating a purely Serbian state." The claim is quite absurd, and leads to obscuring a crucial fact. In the former Yugoslavia, the gravest and most serious crimes of all against international law was committed. It was a crime against peace itself, a sovereign European state was shattered. By adopting this position, the OTP and solves from responsibility the real perpetrators of this crime against peace, the separatist leaderships of the former Yugoslav republics, Slovenia, Croatia, and later, Bosnia-Hercegovina, as well as those international players who backed them throughout this bloody process. By doing this the OTP chooses to ignore some leading principles of international law established by the Nuremberg trials. The shattering of the sovereign state of Yugoslavia by aggression was committed by separatist force who is enjoyed -- who enjoyed the open support of international players. The OTP seems to be neglecting this or glossing over it. They represent this to have been an aggressive war waged by the Serbs of Yugoslavia. The Serbs were peacefully living in Yugoslavia but they tried to show the Serbs as having committed this crime in order to establish a purely Serbian state. Simple facts will do to disprove the allegations of the indictment. The Serbs in the former Yugoslav Republic of Yugoslavia according to the 1991 census made up as many as 581.000 inhabitants of the republic. This is official data. I am not even mentioning the 20.000 people who declared themselves as Yugoslavs, 95 per cent of which were Serbs. Throughout the civil war in the former Yugoslav Republic of Yugoslavia since 1990 and all the way up until the end of 1995, more than 500.000 Serb citizens were expelled. During the military operations, executed by the Croatian police and paramilitary units in the Republic of Serbian Krajina throughout this period of time 7.000 Serbs were killed, 1.100 predominantly Serb villages were razed to the ground. In the Serbian Republic of Krajina, 30.000 Serb houses were destroyed. 50.000 flats were taken from Serbs from the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Serbian Krajina and their tenancy rights were denied, although Croats were allowed to buy the flats under these same conditions. The value of all these flats that were confiscated is estimated at about 30 billion euros. These are real consequences of what happened in the former Yugoslav republics of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. And they are no more than partially reflected in indictments raised before this Tribunal against the Croatian generals, Gotovina, Markac, and Cermak, charged with prosecuting the Serbian population of Krajina during the -- during Operation Storm, which began on the 4th of August 1995 and continued for some time. The indictment faced by six leaders of the Croatian Defence Council and the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina lists the following charges against the accused: There is a whole series of grave and serious crimes involving the political leadership of the Republic of Croatia which intended to create a pan-Croatian state which would have included a great deal of Bosnian territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The genocide against Serbs started in 1990 and continued until 1995. It is only partially addressed in these indictments. The Prosecution mentions the genocide committed by the Axis powers back in the Second World War. Croatia was then part of a fascist alliance and called itself the independent state of Croatia at the time, the MDH. It was a quisling creation which covered today's territories of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. The independent state of Croatia organised and perpetrated a blood-curdling genocide against its Serbian population under the following slogan: "One-third to be killed, one-third to be christened, one third to be expelled." In the concentration camp of Jasenovac alone, 700.000 Serbs were killed as well as 30.000 Jews and Roma. In 1990 and 1991, in the territories of the former Yugoslavia, there was an eruption of separatist movements in both Croatia and Slovenia. On that very same day, the 25th of June 1991, they declared independence, their independence, from Yugoslavia which ran counter to the constitution of Yugoslavia and principles of international law. The Serbs in Croatia found themselves facing an extremely difficult situation at there point in time. According to the then constitution of the Socialist Republic of Croatia, which was still valid in 1991 I quote, "The Socialist Federative Republic of Croatia is a national state of all Croats, all Serbs, and all its ethnic minorities." This is Article 1 of the constitution of the Socialist Federative Republic of Croatia. This constitutional provision was a result of the fact that following the victory of the anti-fascist forces in the Second World War, Orthodox Serbs forgave Croats for the genocide that they had committed against them. They agreed to organise their ethnic Serb territories in cooperation with the Croatian people and establish the people's Republic of Croatia which was later to become the Socialist Republic of Croatia. There was only one condition, however. The condition was that the Croatian authorities would not sever the links between the Serbs in Krajina and the Serbs in other territories of the Croatian state. This provision contained in their own constitution and the political will of Croatia's Serbs was disregarded by the new Croatian government and the new Croatian assembly or parliament. They seceded from Yugoslavia and declared their independence from Yugoslavia, thereby denying a provision from their own constitution about the sovereign position of Serbs in Croatia, thereby denying them a constituent status and turning them into a national minority. The secessionist government of Croatia conducted an aggression from within in the sovereign state of Yugoslavia by blocking the barracks and committing acts of terror against its Serbs. The then president of the HDZ, General Franjo Tudjman, who was to become president of the Republic of Croatia, at the founding assembly of the HDZ in the Lisinski concert hall on the 24th of February 1990 in Zagreb pronounced the following sentence, "The independent state of Croatia was not merely a quisling creation and a fascist crime. It was also an expression of the historical ambition of the Croatian people." And if I may add, a blood-curdling notion to all Serbs in Croatia. Nevertheless, this one sentence was an abridged political platform of the LDZ which found Croatian fanaticism by its political actions. The well respected German magazine, Der Spiegel, covered the imminent elections in Croatia in the following way on the 16th of April 1990. "The HDZ has the greatest chances to win these elections. They represent an extremist group openly dreaming about a sovereign Croatia. They have territorial claims on the neighbouring country of Bosnia-Herzegovina and they are fanning the flames of ethnic hatred against the Serbs. They are led by the former general, Franjo Tudjman, whose ideas very much resemble those of the fascist Croatian state in the Second World War. He advocates an independent Croatia." The Serbs in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia in 1990 and 1991 were shocked by the measures taken by the Croatian government, which were the same as those that were taken in the fascist times. Practically overnight, the Serbs ceased to be a constituent ethnic group in the Republic of Croatia by a decision of the Croatian government. Croatia was proclaimed to be a state of Croatian people only. These were obvious references to the NDH laws from 1941 with Article 2 determining that a member of the NDH could only be a person of Aryan ethnic origin. There were legal provisions on ethnic origin establishing who was to be considered a Jew and who was to be considered a gypsy. These very same provisions were then applied to the letter on the Serbs. In conditions of mass nationalistic hysteria fanned by the HDZ, the Serbs became a target of pogrom and acts of terror in Croatia. The new Croatian authorities requested the Serbs to sign declarations of loyalty in order to be able to be -- to obtain Croat citizenship. Throughout 1990 and 1991, Serb employees were fired en masse from their jobs in Croatia because of failure to comply with the new legal authorities in the Republic of Croatia. That was the alleged reason. All of Croatia's Serbs were inevitably reminded of the legal provisions on the protection of Aryan blood in honour of the Croatian people passed and adopted between 1941 and 1945 in the territory of the independent state of Croatia invoked by Franjo Tudjman in his speech on the 24th of February 1990 as his own and defined by him as a legitimate expression of the historical ambition of the Croatian people. What else could this fact have meant for the Serbs, the fact that they were being fired en masse merely because of their ethnic background and because of their Orthodox faith? The order was reintroduced to establish the ethnic backgrounds of all state officials and this is something that was adopted from the old NDH laws. Your Honours, it is quite clear that as I followed the work of the HDZ and the constitutional changes that were taking place at the time, just like other Serbs in Croatia, I was greatly worried and concerned about these developments. It was because of these reasons and certainly not because of any enterprise, least of all a criminal joint enterprise, that I sided with the Serbs who were being discriminated against. I am proud of there fact. In 1990 and 1991, in the territory of the socialist Federative Republic of Croatia, about 10.000 Serb houses were mined and booby trapped. Flats were taken away by force from their rightful Serb owners, and the same thing happened to Serbs all over again that had happened between 1941 and 1945 in the independent state of Croatia where racial laws were applied and where a legal provision existed on property needing to be declared by all non-Aryan or Jewish owners. This same provision was applied to Serbs as well in the NDH throughout the Second World War. Based on these Aryan laws all of the Serbs' property was taken away and confiscated as though the Serbs were some inferior race. At the founding session of the HDZ on the 24th of February 1990 in Zagreb, Franjo Tudjman brought and gave prime seats, as it were, to prominent criminals from the Second World War who had been hiding from the law somewhere abroad. In Croatia, a climate of general hatred against Serbs is created. Serbs are attacked openly on the state television over the radio, hate speeches are a frequent feature of Croat politicians. As Der Spiegel pointed out back in mid-April 1990, they started creating and encouraging fanatical hatred toward Serbs which were now being insultingly referred to as Chetniks, and this name was not used by accident. The mechanism of propaganda in addition to speeches and activities aimed at spreading fear covered all Serbs. All Serbs without exception were marked as Chetniks. They reversed thesis and they did that on purpose. Chetniks were used in order to insult all Serbs as a nation, because Chetniks in prior wars were known as warriors, thus implying that all Serbs are aggressive murderers prepared to commit murder without notice. And thus, they created a climate in which it was easier to commit a collective crime. In the fascist independent state of Croatia, in the course of the Second World War, Cyrillic alphabet was banned by law.
